name: Anise (Pimpinella anisum)
short: Infants: liver failure, seizures after star anise plus green anise infusion (1 case); salmonella outbreak, tea with contaminated aniseed. Allergy: tongue swelling. Trials: few or no adverse events.
text: This entry covers anise or aniseed (Pimpinella anisum, also called green anise) taken by mouth (as seed powder in the dyspepsia and COVID-19 trials; the menopause trial abstract does not give the form); it is a different plant from star anise. Trials: in a 2-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 225 adults with COVID-19 and gut symptoms (45 given powdered aniseed, 180 placebo), two people on aniseed and three on placebo reported mild to moderate adverse events. In an 8-week randomized trial in 60 menopausal women given anise or placebo, with weekly safety interviews, no adverse effects were observed; liver and kidney tests were done at baseline and after 12 weeks, but the abstract does not report their results. The abstract of a 107-patient functional dyspepsia trial of anise powder reports no safety data. Allergy: case reports describe tongue swelling (angioedema) after drinking an aniseed liqueur, which the authors call the first reported immediate-type (type I) allergy from aniseed liqueur, and an aniseed food allergy confirmed by a double-blind, placebo-controlled oral challenge in a person sensitised to aniseed at work, who had nose and eye symptoms and gut symptoms and whose serum cross-reacted with caraway, coriander, fennel and dill. A review of spice allergy says anise allergy is less common but can be a serious problem because of cross-reactivity with birch pollen. Infants: a nationwide outbreak of Salmonella Agona infection among infants in Germany, from October 2002 to July 2003, was caused by aniseed-containing herbal tea (the report's title calls the aniseed contaminated); in a laboratory typing study, Salmonella Agona bacteria from infants with gastroenteritis in Germany matched those from an untreated batch of aniseed imported from Turkey and from a fennel, aniseed and caraway infusion in tea bags. The harm reported was Salmonella infection, which the report's title attributes to contaminated aniseed. Apart from this outbreak and the case below, no infant data on anise were found. A case report describes liver failure with severe clotting problems, low blood sugar and seizures in a 4-month-old infant given a daily home-made infusion of star anise and green anise for two months; the abstract does not separate the two plants. Reports of infant poisoning from star anise tea are given in the star anise entry. The cited sources give no data on pregnancy. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
